items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we want to write down the infinite geometric series
[MATH: S = 1+ \dfrac 1 2 + \dfrac 1 4 + \dfrac 1 8 + \dfrac{1}{16} + \dots]
in a compact way. We can express this using sigma notation with summation to infinity, as follows:
[MATH: S = \displaystyle\sum_{n = 1}^\infty a_n.]
Let us define [MATH: a_n.] The common ratio for the given series is [MATH: r = \dfrac 1 2] and the first term is [MATH: a_1 = 1.] Therefore, we have

Content:
[MATH: a_{n}|= a_{1} ⋅ r^{n − 1}; = ((1)/(2))^{n − 1}; = ((1)/(2))^{n} ⋅ ((1)/(2))^{− 1}; = 2((1)/(2))^{n}.]

Content:
Finally, the infinite geometric series can be written in sigma notation as
[MATH: S = \displaystyle\sum_{n =1}^\infty 2\left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^{n} .]

Express the sum to infinity of the following geometric series using sigma notation:
[MATH: \dfrac{5}{3}-\dfrac{5}{9}+\dfrac{5}{27}-\dfrac{5}{81}+\cdots]

sections.normalized_html:
The first term [MATH: a_1 = \dfrac{5}{3}] and the second term [MATH: a_2 = - \dfrac{5}{9}.] Using these two terms, we compute the common ratio: [MATH: r = \frac{a_2}{a_1} = \frac{\left(-\dfrac{5}{9} \right)}{\left(\dfrac{5}{3} \right)} = - \dfrac{1}{3}.]

Therefore, the general term [MATH: a_n] can be expressed as [MATH: a_{n}|= a_{1}(r)^{n − 1}; = (5)/(3)(− (1)/(3))^{n − 1}; = (5)/(3)(− (1)/(3))^{− 1}(− (1)/(3))^{n}; = (− 5)(− (1)/(3))^{n}.]

Finally, the infinite geometric series can be written in sigma notation as [MATH: (5)/(3) − (5)/(9) + (5)/(27) − (5)/(81) + ⋯|= ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)a_{n}; = ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)(− 5)(− (1)/(3))^{n}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

[MATH: S = 1+ \dfrac 1 2 + \dfrac 1 4 + \dfrac 1 8 + \dfrac{1}{16} + \dots]
in a compact way. We can express this using sigma notation with summation to infinity, as follows:
[MATH: S = \displaystyle\sum_{n = 1}^\infty a_n.]
Let us define [MATH: a_n.] The common ratio for the given series is [MATH: r = \dfrac 1 2] and the first term is [MATH: a_1 = 1.] Therefore, we have

Content:
[MATH: a_{n}|= a_{1} ⋅ r^{n − 1}; = ((1)/(2))^{n − 1}; = ((1)/(2))^{n} ⋅ ((1)/(2))^{− 1}; = 2((1)/(2))^{n}.]

Finally, the infinite geometric series can be written in sigma notation as

Item 2 — Example: Expressing an Infinite Series Using Sigma Notation Given The First Few Terms

Example Prompt:
Express the sum to infinity of the following geometric series using sigma notation:
[MATH: \dfrac{5}{3}-\dfrac{5}{9}+\dfrac{5}{27}-\dfrac{5}{81}+\cdots]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The first term [MATH: a_1 = \dfrac{5}{3}] and the second term [MATH: a_2 = - \dfrac{5}{9}.] Using these two terms, we compute
the common ratio:
[MATH: r = \frac{a_2}{a_1} = \frac{\left(-\dfrac{5}{9} \right)}{\left(\dfrac{5}{3} \right)} = - \dfrac{1}{3}.]

Therefore, the general term [MATH: a_n] can be expressed as
[MATH: a_{n}|= a_{1}(r)^{n − 1}; = (5)/(3)(− (1)/(3))^{n − 1}; = (5)/(3)(− (1)/(3))^{− 1}(− (1)/(3))^{n}; = (− 5)(− (1)/(3))^{n}.]

Finally, the infinite geometric series can be written in sigma notation as
[MATH: (5)/(3) − (5)/(9) + (5)/(27) − (5)/(81) + ⋯|= ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)a_{n}; = ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)(− 5)(− (1)/(3))^{n}.]
